title: Sirloin steak on the bone seared in reverse gear
summary: There aren’t many recipes for meat that combine the slow food ethos with that of grilling something over very high heat, but both techniques come into play for reverse-searing a steak. It turns the traditional way of doing so upside down: y
content:
There aren’t many recipes for meat that combine the slow food ethos with that of grilling something over very high heat, but both techniques come into play for reverse-searing a steak. It turns the traditional way of doing so upside down: you start by cooking it in a ridiculously low oven or kettle braai, or high above hardly any coals at all, and you finish it with a short, sharp hellfire sear to get that lovely golden and crunchy outer coating that all true steak lovers adore; the umami of the burn that makes such magic on the palate.

My good friend Gordon Wright introduced me to the notion of a reverse-seared steak in person as well as in his best-selling books, Veld to Fork and Karoo Food. Not that the Karoo can claim reverse-searing as its own, but it does somehow fit in with the pace of life in those towns and plains.

Gordon, like many contemporary cooks, owns a meat thermometer which he actually uses. I own one too, I think – somewhere, maybe – but I’ve never got into the habit of using it. I’m an old-fashioned boy and an old-fashioned cook, and I like a tactile approach. I use my instincts, nose and sense of touch. That’s when I’ll know it’s been slow-cooked for long enough without going too far, and be ready for that final sear. In Karoo Food, his second book, there is a fearsome chart for reverse-searing a tomahawk steak in a kettle braai, and another for reverse-searing a rib-eye using the oven and pan method. It sets out the target temperatures in the kettle or oven for rare, medium-rare, medium and medium-well, then gives the final target temperature and approximate time in the oven for each. That’s all far too technical for the likes of me.

The key is this, and it’s emphatic: the steak must be thick-cut, not less than 3cm to 5cm, preferably more; for the tomahawk recipe they should be 5cm to 8cm thick, or more. It needs some good fat on it too, to take advantage of the lusciously moreish tender centre while scorching it on the outside later on to crusty-fatty perfection. And the steaks should be well aged, none of those bright-red bushy-tailed ones for this method. It’s the brownish hue of age that you want. Virtually on the turn? Even better!

_Reprint! Tony Jackman’s Retro Karoo Food (Penguin Random House) is off to the printers for its second reprint since being published in March 2026. To purchase a copy signed by the author, send an email to him at_[_tony@dailymaverick.co.za._](mailto:tony@dailymaverick.co.za)_Or buy it through the_[_Daily Maverick shop_](https://shop.dailymaverick.co.za/product/retro-karoo-food-80-nostalgic-south-african-recipes/)_._

The sirloin steaks in this recipe were 4cm thick, and being on the bone meant they could only lend more flavour and depth. Gordon warns that there is no value in using the reverse-sear method for a thin steak since they cook too fast, defeating the object.

The MasterClass.com website espouses three benefits of the reverse sear for a steak: an evenly cooked interior; a browned, crispy crust, and flavourful pan drippings. Conversely, in the traditional method, your chef will sear and seal the steak first and then finish it gently in the oven to cook it to the level you like.

And the reverse-sear method can be used for chicken cuts and pork chops too; again, choose breasts on the bone and thick-cut pork loin chops for best results. The steak cuts that MasterClass recommends for the technique are rib-eye, tomahawk, tri-tip (picanha), T-bone, porterhouse (sirloin), New York strip (short loin) and filet mignon (the thinner end of the loin). I would add to that the Chateaubriand, being the thicker, fatter part of the beef fillet, which strikes me as being ideal for reverse-searing, given its thickness.

### Tony’s reverse-seared sirloin steak on the bone

**Ingredients**

2 x matured 700g thick-cut sirloins on the bone (ours were 4cm thick)

2 Tbsp fresh rosemary needles, finely chopped

2 garlic cloves, finely chopped

1 Tbsp rosemary salt

⅓ cup olive oil

Zest of 1 ripe lemon

½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper

**Method**

Remove steaks from the fridge an hour before you need to start cooking them.

Stir the rosemary needles, chopped garlic and lemon zest into the olive oil.

Brush this over both sides of the steaks, retaining the rest for basting while cooking.

Season both sides generously with rosemary salt and pepper.

Leave them to absorb those flavours, at room temperature, while you light a fire in one part of a braai while leaving another part free for the slow cook. You’ll need to ensure a red-hot supply of coals for when the time comes to do the sear.

Transfer a few coals to the edges of the area you’re using for the first cook. Place the grid high above it, and a pan for drippings at the bottom.

Put the steaks on the grid and turn frequently to ensure a very slow cook, for about 30 to 45 minutes depending on the thickness of the meat.

Use the good old-fashioned finger test as I do (you get a feel for it, literally); it’s a pliable tenderness to the touch that you’re after. If you’re using a thermometer, you’re looking for an inner temperature of about 50℃. Again, I’d sooner trust my fingers.

Keep the steaks to one side, uncovered and in the ambient temperature but not close to heat, and set over the dripping pan to catch any more juices. It doesn’t matter that they cool down, they’re going to be finished over high heat anyway.

Shovel hot coals where the dripping pan was (which you have removed), lower the grid and sear those fat steaks for 3 minutes on each side.

If using an oven, first cook them for 30 to 45 minutes at 120℃ and cook over a dripping pan for medium rare, before doing a quick sear in a very hot skillet or on hot coals for 3 minutes per side.

Use the dripping to make a sauce in a pot on the stove. Deglaze the pan with liquid beef stock, add a glass of red wine and reduce it to thicken. Season with rosemary salt and pepper. **DM**

_Tony Jackman is twice winner of the Galliova Food Writer of the Year award._

_Follow Tony Jackman on Instagram_[_@tony\_jackman\_cooks_](https://www.instagram.com/tony_jackman_cooks/)_._

title: Can SA teams break Champions Cup semifinal ceiling?
summary: South African clubs have added enormous value to the United Rugby Championship (URC) since joining the northern hemisphere tournament in 2021, but are yet to make a meaningful impact on the European Champions Cup. After four seasons, no Sou
content:
South African clubs have added enormous value to the United Rugby Championship (URC) since joining the northern hemisphere tournament in 2021, but are yet to make a meaningful impact on the European Champions Cup.

After four seasons, no South African side has managed to progress beyond the quarterfinal stage of the world’s leading club tournament, and a playoff victory on European soil remains elusive.

Critics from the north have hammered South African clubs after they’ve fielded weakened teams in the pool phase and sustained heavy losses.

More measured commentators have observed that South African rugby is caught between a rock and a hard place, with the player management challenge exacerbated by a neverending season as well as an extraordinary travel schedule that often sees teams bouncing between Africa and Europe weekly.

Elliot Daly of Saracens and Makazole Mapimpi of the Sharks in action during a Champions Cup match at Kings Park Stadium on 13 December 2025. (Photo: Steve Haag Sports / Gallo Images / Getty Images)

### Banking points, boxing clever

The player management and travel challenges of the past four seasons have prevented local clubs from performing in two tournaments simultaneously – and has often forced them to prioritise the URC over the Champions Cup.

There’s a growing fear that the 2026/27 edition will serve up another series of humbling results.

This season, the clubs will face the additional challenge of managing their Springboks with next year’s World Cup in mind. Following the club playoffs next June, the Boks will play six Rugby Championship Tests, before focusing on the global tournament in Australia, which kicks off in October.

All that said, there may be reason to hope for a more competitive performance at home and abroad – at least by the leading teams – and perhaps a historic appearance in the semifinals.

The Bulls and Stormers are unlikely to beat the likes of Bordeaux-Bégles and Leinster in the race for the Champions Cup title, but they may show the rugby world why South Africa deserves a seat at the top table.

While South African coaches have copped a lot of criticism for selecting weakened teams for pool fixtures staged overseas, the reality is that most clubs back their best combinations in home matches and send heavily rotated sides abroad.

The key difference is that the better teams tend to bank four or five log points in both home fixtures and do enough to salvage one or two points in games staged on the road.

Stormers centre Dan du Plessis on the charge against La Rochelle at Cape Town Stadium on 6 April 2024. (Photo: Grant Pitcher / Gallo Images / Getty Images)

No team goes into this tournament expecting to win every pool game – especially when they’re juggling their resources across other competitions such as the URC, the English Premiership and the French Top 14 – and the better coaches know how to box cleverly.

Every contender is looking for enough log points to secure a home quarterfinal, and to avoid an overseas playoff which can lead to further player-management and travel complications down the line.

### Bulls, Stormers to fly SA flag again

The Bulls and Stormers both progressed to the Champions Cup round of 16 last season, but ultimately paid the price for their inconsistent showings across the pool phase.

Johan Ackermann’s charges were forced to travel to Glasgow for the first round of the playoffs, and while they pushed the Warriors close, they went down 25-21. The Stormers produced a spirited performance in the Stade Mayol bear pit but lost 28-27 to Toulon.

While both performances were lauded within the South African community, Ackermann and Stormers boss John Dobson conceded they were always going to be underdogs in playoffs staged overseas.

Since then, both coaches have worked harder to bolster their squads with more Boks and senior players with experience of European conditions. They are in a better position to compete in this tournament than was the case last season.

The structure of the tournament has been altered this year, with the first round staged this weekend – instead of early December – and the second scheduled to commence on 11 December. The change may mitigate some of the player-management challenges and ensure that all teams give the tournament the attention it deserves.

Le Roux Malan of the Sharks carries against ASM Clermont Auvergne at Kings Park on 17 January 2026. (Photo: Steve Haag Sports / Gallo Images)

The Bulls should be aiming to lay down a marker against Stade Francais in Pretoria this Saturday. Their second fixture in Montpellier will be more demanding, given that the French side won the Challenge Cup last season and were Top 14 finalists.

It won’t get any easier when they face Johann van Graan’s Bath at home in early January or when they travel to Northampton Saints, the reigning Prem champions, the following week.

The Stormers have the benefit of starting their campaign at home, and despite the attacking threat of Bristol, the ambitious Cape side should be aiming for five log points. They couldn’t have asked for a tougher fixture in round two, given that they will head to Bordeaux to face the two-time champions.

In January, Dobson’s charges will face Gloucester away and Racing 92 at home, and given the number of Boks at their disposal and the relative strength of the opposition, they should expect to win both fixtures. Gloucester currently lead the Prem table, but have battled to compete in Europe, while Racing are ranked 12th in the Top 14 at present.

The Lions will make their Champions Cup debut when they face former winners La Rochelle in France this Saturday, and they could be in for a baptism of fire.

Lions coach Cash van Rooyen. (Photo: Lefty Shivambu / Gallo Images)

While the Lions have taken giant strides over the past season, they may not have the depth to maintain their effort across four games and qualify for the Champions Cup playoffs. Their poor overseas record does not bode well for another testing away fixture at Saracens in January.

Cash van Rooyen’s side should be more competitive against Toulon in Johannesburg in round two, and against Exeter Chiefs in the next home match in round four.

Two home wins may be viewed as a fair return in their inaugural campaign. They don’t have the depth of the Bulls or Stormers and may struggle to meet the demands of competing in both the URC and the Champions Cup.

### Sharks’ fight for redemption

Given their resources, the Sharks should be the leading team in the country and South Africa’s best bet for silverware.

And yet, the Durban-based club has failed to qualify for the Champions Cup on two occasions over the past five years. They were relegated to the Challenge Cup after a poor URC campaign last season, and face a fight for redemption in the coming months.

The Sharks will qualify for the next edition of the Champions Cup if they win the Challenge Cup outright – as they did in 2024 – or if they finish the URC league phase in the top seven.

They face a potentially tricky match in Lyon this Saturday. A win would set them up for the rest of the Challenge Cup pool phase, given that they will face the Scarlets and Castres at home in the next two games. They may fancy their chances in their final away fixture in Treviso, given that they play Benetton regularly in the URC.

It remains to be seen whether the Cheetahs will progress to the Challenge Cup playoffs. Frans Steyn’s team will travel to Bayonne this Sunday, before facing the Dragons, Zebre and Perpignan in later rounds. Due to their status as an invitational side, the Free State outfit will play their second and fourth fixtures at St Helens in Swansea, Wales. **DM**

title: Pensioner builds her own home as government project stalls
summary: When the government told Nomonde Mboyi, 67, three years ago that it would build her a new house after hers was destroyed in a storm, she didn’t bother waiting. She started building her own house, using mud bricks she made herself and using
content:
When the government told Nomonde Mboyi, 67, three years ago that it would build her a new house after hers was destroyed in a storm, she didn’t bother waiting. She started building her own house, using mud bricks she made herself and using her old-age grant to buy materials and pay for labour. Since then, the government project has stalled.

Mboyi’s was one of hundreds of households that lost their homes during heavy winds and rain in the Mbizana region of the rural Eastern Cape in 2019. She lost two mud houses. A third house, built from sticks and mud, was left with a leaking roof and holes in its walls.

In 2023, the Eastern Cape Department of Human Settlements appointed ZIBSIPRO (Pty) Ltd to replace the storm-damaged houses with 200 houses across the region for about R34-million – about R170,000 per house. But not one of the houses has been completed.

The brick-and-mortar house the government is building for Mboyi only has a foundation and partially completed walls. This is the case at most of the houses under construction in Mboyi’s village, Ndakeni.

“When the contractor came here last year to start the foundation, I was already starting the walls of my two-room house. I used my social grant to buy materials and pay for labour. But the process was not quick because I had to spend months saving enough money before I could continue,” she said.

Her new mud house just needs plastering outside and some final touch-ups before she moves in in December. She said Eskom cannot install electricity because the house is not waterproof.

### ‘Told to wait’

Mboyi said that, during a meeting with the Winnie Madikizela-Mandela Local Municipality in February this year, residents offered to finish building the houses themselves, but were told to wait.

“Since then, there has been no further explanation. We are just waiting,” she said.

Community leader Nontokozo Nyombo said many of the beneficiaries, who mostly relied on social grants, were in desperate need of housing.

“People are very frustrated, and the sad thing is that we don’t know who to turn to. Our municipality no longer gives us answers on the matter,” she said.

Residents said the contractor left in November last year, promising to return, but had not done so. There is still some construction machinery in the village, watched over by a security guard.

Department spokesperson Yanga Funani said ZIBSIPRO’s contract was terminated during the 2025/26 financial year because of poor performance.

He said the department planned to reinstate the project. Houses where construction had already started would be prioritised, and those not yet started would be dependent on funding availability.

But ZIBSIPRO director Palesa Phara said she was not aware the contract had been terminated. She claimed that non-payment by the department had made it financially impossible to continue. However, she acknowledged that the department had sent the company a letter of default and that the company tried to cede the work to a subcontractor, which the department verbally rejected.

“All I know is that the department has owed us payment for a year, which is why I stopped working with them,” she said.

Phara said the company was appointed in September 2023, but only received a formal contract towards the end of November, shortly before the annual construction shutdown.

Work could not start immediately, she said. Geotechnical investigations, soil assessments and approval processes delayed construction further. The approved foundation design was also “heavily over-engineered” and the company hired another engineer to redesign it.

Conditional approvals from the National Home Builders Registration Council were also required before work could proceed.

### Logistical challenges

She said construction effectively began around October 2024, more than a year after the company was appointed. She also said working across 34 villages created logistical challenges, while heavy rain disrupted construction.

Phara also alleged that the company was verbally instructed to “slow down” because the department did not have sufficient funds available. Also, the payment arrangements changed from paying at each building stage (milestones) to paying only when a unit was finished, she said. This placed financial pressure on the company, which had to keep buying materials and paying workers without receiving corresponding payments.

“Eventually, site operations became unsafe. Certain labourers, local workers, security personnel and community stakeholders effectively prevented further access to the site until outstanding [labour] disputes and payments were resolved,” she said.

“Some company equipment and infrastructure remain on site to this day, continuing to generate storage and security costs while also remaining inaccessible,” she said.

Funani did not respond to Phara’s allegations. The municipality did not respond to our questions, referring us to the department. **DM**

_Originally published by_[_GroundUp_](https://groundup.org.za/article/tired-waiting-for-government-pensioner-builds-her-own-house-using-sassa-grants/)_._

title: Lukhona Mnguni’s pitch for a Joburg that belongs to everyone
summary: There are probably worse ways to make a case for serendipity in Johannesburg’s politics than having Fikile Mbalula walk into a restaurant just as you are discussing the coalitions that could determine who becomes the city’s next mayor. [Luk
content:
There are probably worse ways to make a case for serendipity in Johannesburg’s politics than having Fikile Mbalula walk into a restaurant just as you are discussing the coalitions that could determine who becomes the city’s next mayor.

[Lukhona Mnguni](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-05-22-rise-mzansis-lukhona-mnguni-enters-joburg-mayoral-race-warns-of-gangster-state/) was explaining who Rise Mzansi could and could not work with after the election when the ANC secretary-general appeared at Tashas at The Marc in Sandton. The two greeted each other warmly before Mnguni asked when the [ANC](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-09-01-five-signs-the-anc-has-given-up-on-joburg/) was finally going to give Johannesburg its mayoral candidate. Mbalula smiled, gestured towards him and joked that the mayor was already there.

“What are the odds of talking about coalitions, and then the people we might be negotiating with actually pitch up?” Mnguni laughed after the encounter. “Maybe a coalition has just been sealed in Tashas at The Marc.”

Mnguni describes himself as a spiritual person who believes serendipitous moments happen for a reason. He also calls himself “a villager caught in urban trappings”, a phrase that fits neatly with the Johannesburg he is campaigning to lead: a city of very different worlds pressed up against one another, sometimes uneasily, but still dependent on one another.

He had originally wanted to meet at [Kwa Mai Mai](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2024-09-20-no-frills-or-fuss-is-apparently-the-secret-to-a-good-shisanyama/). Instead, sitting in Sandton, in what is commonly called Africa’s richest square mile, he spoke fondly about the traditional market opposite Maboneng, where people buy food, traditional goods and muti and where, he insisted, some of Joburg’s best scones are baked.

“It holds a lot of nostalgia for Joburgers. You get a sense of home, a bit of home,” he said, before pointing to the contrast between the development on one side of the road and neglect on the other. “It’s a pity that when Maboneng was being developed, Kwa Mai Mai was left behind because it’s literally right opposite.”

That contrast offers a useful way into Mnguni’s politics, which repeatedly come back to whether Johannesburg can function as one city rather than a collection of neighbourhoods whose access to safety, opportunity and basic services depends on geography and income.

Lukhona Mnguni chats about his vision for Johannesburg. (Photo: Our City News / James Oatway)

It also shapes his view of migration, with Mnguni describing Johannesburg as a city “built by migrants from all over the continent” and arguing that tensions between South Africans and migrants were tied to competition over jobs and failing public services.

He supports immigration enforcement and documentation [requirements for traders](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-02-23-barred-joburg-informal-traders-cant-pay-pay-school-fees-as-city-permit-confusion/), but said the Johannesburg Metro Police Department (JMPD) should not be “criminalising poor people” or pushing informal businesses to places where they cannot survive.

His position became more radical when discussing [hostels](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2025-08-13-residents-demand-more-than-renovations-in-johannesburgs-hostels-in-call-for-true-transformation/), saying that the apartheid-era model had failed and should ultimately be replaced with better housing, and that many hostels had become spaces with poor living conditions, violence and political control.

### Rebuilding Joburg’s systems

Serendipity may make for good political theatre, but Mnguni knows Johannesburg cannot be repaired through spiritual conviction and fortunate encounters alone. His campaign ultimately rests on a more practical argument. It revolves around the idea that fixing the city means rebuilding the systems that determine how safely people live, how reliably services work, and how easily residents can reach jobs and opportunity.

That thinking also runs through Rise Mzansi’s broader plan for Johannesburg. Its Spatial Justice proposals focus on bringing people closer to jobs and economic opportunity through better-located housing. At the same time, A Living City aims to make streets safer, cleaner and more workable for the residents and informal traders who use them every day.

For Mnguni, these are symptoms of a city so accustomed to failure that residents and institutions increasingly work around broken systems rather than expecting them to be repaired.

> “It’s almost like we have now planned for the collapse, and we are accommodating the collapse,” he said.

The remaining campaign pillars try to address that failure more directly. Dignity in Every Ward promises a minimum standard of municipal services regardless of neighbourhood, while Infrastructure Reliability focuses on water, electricity and the maintenance of ageing networks. Jozi On the Move centres on integrated, safer and more affordable public transport that connects residents more easily to work and opportunity.

Mnguni said a government led by him would prove its case in 70 days rather than the conventional first 100 days benchmark. That is because his administration would immediately have to deal with Johannesburg’s adjusted budget. He wants bid evaluation and adjudication meetings recorded and eventually made public, along with a water master plan, accelerated pipe replacement and a more intensive approach to waste management.

“You cannot develop the city if you don’t invest meaningfully in the water infrastructure,” he said. “We need to reduce the leaks. A lot of water is running on the streets and not running in the taps.”

### **‘**A 10 to 15-year plan’

Mnguni is also unusually willing, for a candidate asking voters to hand him the City, to acknowledge that Johannesburg’s decline is too deep to reverse within a single term.

“Definitely, the turnaround of Joburg is a 10- to 15-year plan. So much has deteriorated,” he said. “You won’t get to every neighbourhood within five years. But I think you could, in five years time, tell a different story about the City of Joburg.”

That story, in his telling, is not only about pipes, roads or municipal finances. Mnguni argues that residents have not abandoned Johannesburg even if many have lost faith in those governing it, pointing to [residents’ associations](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2025-09-04-communities-repair-roads-water-and-power-in-diy-revolution-as-city-of-joburg-falters/), neighbourhood WhatsApp groups and businesses increasingly filling the gaps left by the municipality.

“If people were not involved, this city would probably have collapsed by now... What I think people have lost is confidence in electoral politics,” he said.

The Orlando Pirates shirt he wore to the interview offered a lighter expression of the same attachment to the city. Asked whether it risked alienating Kaizer Chiefs supporters, Mnguni joked that “you can’t alienate your own children”, before recalling how he fell for Pirates during their 1995 African Champions League triumph. Kaizer Chiefs broke away from Pirates.

For him, clubs such as Pirates, Chiefs and Moroka Swallows are part of Johannesburg’s civic memory, institutions rooted in communities and in the stories people tell about the city. That is why he talks about sport not simply as recreation, but as part of rebuilding social life and creating opportunities for young people whose talent could otherwise be lost.

Mnguni linked that erosion of community directly to Johannesburg’s crime problem, arguing that safer neighbourhoods would require both a better-resourced JMPD and a city where residents felt comfortable occupying public spaces again.

“When we are unsafe, we go to our private spaces. But when we retreat to our private spaces, we deplete the community,” he said, adding that: “When we deplete a community, we open up much more space for criminality.”

Whether Mnguni gets the opportunity to put any of these ideas into practice will depend heavily on the coalition negotiations that follow the election. He has ruled out the Patriotic Alliance, but not the ANC or DA, and says coalition partners should be bound by a public programme and anti-corruption agreement rather than negotiations over positions. (See the current polling numbers below.)

“We cannot create a coalition where we are trying to parcel out who becomes the board chairperson of which entity, who becomes the CEO of which entity.

“We’re not going to be in the business of deal-making. We are going to be in the business of governing the City of Johannesburg in the best interests of the residents,” he said. **DM**

_This interview is part of an ongoing series by Our City News featuring key mayoral candidates contesting the City of Johannesburg in the upcoming local government elections._

title: Climate change-HIV connection and how to report on it
summary: On 12 April 2022, Mfundo Shezi woke when the skies cracked open and unleashed a merciless[deluge over KwaZulu-Natal](https://bhekisisa.org/special-reports/climate-change/2025-09-22-the-falling-down-place/). The 32-year-old, who usually slee
content:
On 12 April 2022, Mfundo Shezi woke when the skies cracked open and unleashed a merciless[deluge over KwaZulu-Natal](https://bhekisisa.org/special-reports/climate-change/2025-09-22-the-falling-down-place/). The 32-year-old, who usually sleeps in a park in Umbilo in Durban, immediately fled for shelter, abandoning all he owned.

Shezi didn’t have much, but by the time he returned the next morning, he found that the flood had taken all of his possessions. That included his ID and his monthly supply of[antiretroviral (ARV) treatment](https://www.cdc.gov/hiv/basics/livingwithhiv/treatment.html) for HIV, which he had been taking faithfully since he started treatment in 2021.

“On that day, I missed a dose for the first time,” he[told Bhekisisa](https://bhekisisa.org/article/2022-11-17-i-missed-a-dose-for-the-first-time-how-the-kzn-floods-derailed-hiv-treatment/). Without taking his HIV medications consistently, he knew he’d get sick.

He panicked. He tried to get to the local clinic but wasn’t able to get there. So Shezi walked to the government hospital. It was open, but without his ID book – or a transfer letter from his regular clinic, which would allow him to get his medication – they couldn’t help.

Experts say a[changing climate](https://www.un.org/en/climatechange/what-is-climate-change) will probably bring on more bouts of severe weather like this flood, which killed more than 450 people. But the flood itself would not somehow make Shezi’s HIV more infectious or deadly. What changed was everything affected by it: the destroyed roads, the paper file that held his treatment history, the proof he was who he said he was.

Between 2010 and 2023, new[HIV infections fell by almost 60%](https://www.unaids.org/sites/default/files/media_asset/2024-unaids-global-aids-update_en.pdf) in Africa, meaning that for every 10 people who were getting HIV in 2010, four got it in 2023. But the region could start losing those gains as climate shocks collide with[shrinking HIV funding](https://bhekisisa.org/health-news-south-africa/2026-02-05-what-will-hiv-funding-look-like-in-2026/).

Climate scientist[Christopher Jack](https://www.csag.uct.ac.za/author/cjack/), deputy director of the Climate System Analysis Group at the University of Cape Town, and public health specialist[Coceka Nogoduka](https://www.linkedin.com/in/coceka-nogoduka-58026a96/), who, for 18 years, has helped to shape how South Africa deals with HIV and tuberculosis, spoke to a group of journalists in a[Bhekisisa webinar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NtkddBhEJX4&t=20s) on the links between climate change and HIV, what it means and what can be done to get ahead of it. Here’s what we learned.

### Seven key connections

**1. Climate change does not make HIV more infectious**

Extreme heat, rain or drier conditions don’t make the virus more infectious or make people with HIV sicker. But it can[change people’s behaviour](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7810285/) and how, when and where they can get healthcare and medication.

**2. A warmer world could mean far more HIV**

If the world keeps pumping[greenhouse gases](https://wmo.int/topics/greenhouse-gases) such as carbon dioxide and methane into the air at the rate it is now, the average global temperature could, in a[worst-case scenario](https://www.carbonbrief.org/explainer-the-high-emissions-rcp8-5-global-warming-scenario/), be[5°C higher](https://sos.noaa.gov/catalog/datasets/climate-model-temperature-change-rcp-85-2006-2100/) than it was about 150 years ago.

If the air becomes that much warmer,[25-37% more people](https://link.springer.com/epdf/10.1007/s10584-020-02753-y?sharing_token=YQDHvAjqoziQRHk7PocWQ_e4RwlQNchNByi7wbcMAY5R9-bA9E9zn66vTSgGKi-DMwuqVeGJnPpC-bOEbU4UB9Zq5mPUVSkKVV9GlabNbooRhoxUCdCj1sv-tDiKPvWt1WGaKbjeY3_E12gGppB5PWg5DdUHSq4pOBZpRb8iWUc%3D) in sub-Saharan Africa might have HIV by 2050 than would have been expected without such harsh global warming, a modelling study shows.

Meanwhile, every time a bad drought hits – when there is less than 20% of the normally expected rainfall – HIV infections could[climb by 11%](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ecoj.12149) in rural areas in Africa, where many people already have HIV. Heavy rainfall and flooding can increase the[chances of getting HIV by 14%, and make it 11% more](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12039729/) likely for someone to get another sexually transmitted infection.

In the rest of our story, we explain why.

**3. When disaster forces people to move, normal treatment breaks**

Even when weather experts know a flood is on the way, people may still have to flee their homes suddenly. When that happens, they might lose their ID or find it impossible to get to their usual clinic, breaking the daily routine they need to stay healthy with HIV. In 2025, natural disasters across sub-Saharan Africa forced people to move nearly[3 million times](https://api.internal-displacement.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/IDMC-GRID-2026-Global-Report-on-Internal-Displacement.pdf?_gl=1*5pvl8x*_ga*MTUzODA0NTg1NS4xNzc5MjY3MTQx*_ga_PKVS5L6N8V*czE3NzkyNjcxNDEkbzEkZzEkdDE3NzkyNjcxNTUkajQ2JGwwJGgw).

When people are displaced by extreme weather, their homes might be washed away with their identification documents, and they might not even be able to get into a new health facility and be able to identify themselves so that they can then be re-registered into our public health systems. – Coceka Nogoduka

For someone on treatment, that routine is a matter of life and death. If they can’t collect[medication regularly](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11800643/), the virus can get a foothold and start[multiplying](https://www.niaid.nih.gov/diseases-conditions/10-things-know-about-hiv-suppression), making people sick and able to[infect others](https://hivrisk.cdc.gov/can-increase-hiv-risk/).

**4. When people move, their medical records usually don’t**

South Africa has long planned a[national electronic patient record system](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10311353/) that would allow a person’s patient file to follow them if they move and seek care at a different clinic or hospital. But 10 years after it was[first proposed](https://nstiip.naci.org.za/knowledge-base/reports/573-e-health-strategy-south-africa-2012-2016-2/viewdocument/573), that system is not yet fully in place; only the Western Cape has a fully rolled out system in place. In most clinics, patient records are still kept on paper. Even if someone can get a transfer letter, which is needed to get treatment at a different clinic, they may be counted as someone who has stopped taking their medication in one place and considered a brand-new patient in another – something which could not only affect patient care but also[skew how HIV cases are counted](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10022370/) in national registers.

**5. Surviving a disaster can drive risky behaviour**

Women who move because extreme weather has destroyed their livelihood or their access to food are more likely to[trade sex for basic necessities](https://journals.lww.com/jaids/abstract/2022/08010/associations_between_mobility,_food_insecurity,.4.aspx) such as food or shelter.

When someone has to trade sex just to survive, they often lose their say in the relationship. Because they are relying on that partner for their basic needs, the power imbalance makes it much harder for them to insist on using a condom or to have safer sex. Research shows that when women are forced into these survival strategies, they are[twice as likely to get HIV](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9909688/).

**6. Repeated shocks wear down the system**

Stopping HIV needs both treatment and prevention in place – testing, clinic visits and offering condoms or[HIV prevention medication such as the daily anti-HIV pill or six-monthly HIV prevention shot, lenacapavir. HIV prevention meds lower someone’s chances of contracting the virus to close to zero.](https://www.who.int/teams/global-hiv-hepatitis-and-stis-programmes/hiv/prevention/pre-exposure-prophylaxis)Weather disasters put health systems under pressure: clinics close because they are flooded or have no power to keep medicines at the right temperature, and flooded roads and broken bridges stop delivery trucks from reaching remote areas. During major floods in[Namibia’s Ohangwena region in 2009](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1gFi1Li3X6gXj6sXlIXgmpj23ks1xJZFP/view?usp=sharing), damaged roads and floodwaters made 41 health facilities unreachable.

How many more HIV cases [could climate change bring](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-57530-1)?

When HIV-negative people can’t access their next HIV prevention medication dose in time, they’re[no longer protected against the virus](https://bhekisisa.org/health-news-south-africa/2026-09-16-want-the-six-monthly-hiv-jab-heres-your-nine-step-clinic-cheat-sheet/)and their chances of getting HIV increase.

While one flood or drought won’t undo decades of HIV progress, South Africa’s high number of[people living with HIV](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9165791/), alongside more[frequent and intense weather](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211464525000491) and sharp decreases in[HIV funding](https://bhekisisa.org/health-news-south-africa/2025-04-17-r2-82-billion-thats-what-we-need-to-plug-the-us-funding-gap-for-now/), means we’ll be even more vulnerable when the next climate shock lands.

Often we have inadequate infrastructure. The roads are not built well, or not well maintained, and bridges aren’t designed for extreme rainfall events. This often compounds with weak health systems; a non-climate driver is now compounded with this climate impact. These cascade through the system, through infrastructure, through access to healthcare, through health outcomes, and then beyond that into livelihoods, loss of primary breadwinners, and the education system. – Christopher Jack

**7. What could help**

Records that follow a patient would keep treatment going when people move. Health facilities can be built to withstand shocks, and leaders can be held to plans already on the books.

[South Africa’s Climate Change Act](https://cer.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Climate-Change-Act-22-of-2024.pdf) came into operation on 17 March 2025, with a national adaptation strategy meant to follow within a year to help guide how the country prepares and responds.

After Cyclone Freddy swept away paper health documents, medicines and supplies in Malawi in 2023, its former health minister,[Khumbize Kandodo Chiponda, acknowledged it as a failure](https://www.newsweek.com/climate-crisis-escalates-building-resilient-health-systems-imperative-opinion-1843797) of the health system that should be urgently reformed. She set about introducing digitised health records, stronger emergency planning and health facilities that can withstand shocks – an example of how accountability can spur change.

### Connections and angles

Climate change and HIV are connected in many ways – and that’s often where the stories are. Here are some ideas on where to look and what to keep in mind.

**Before and after:** Talk to community members to find out how they were affected, and to healthcare providers, clinic managers and provincial health departments about what happened to patients after recent floods or droughts. Ask:

*   Were clinics accessible after severe weather?

*   Were drug supplies delayed?

*   Did testing or PrEP services pause?

*   Did more patients miss their HIV medication pickups?

*   Were people able to transfer smoothly from one clinic to another?

**Survey systems:** Find the gaps in transport, healthcare and medicine supply chains and the movement of people. That can give concrete examples of system failures that need to be addressed.

title: ‘Hunger has no party’: Election candidates talk to Soweto
summary: “Hunger has no party” was the rallying cry at a Union Against Hunger community meeting, where people asked mayoral candidates and prospective ward councillors how they will solve hunger in Johannesburg. It was a hot day in the community hal
content:
“Hunger has no party” was the rallying cry at a Union Against Hunger community meeting, where people asked mayoral candidates and prospective ward councillors how they will solve hunger in Johannesburg.

It was a hot day in the community hall in Orlando East, Soweto. Some political parties arrived late for the 10am start. At the start, half the hall was empty – much like the [voting booths may be on 4 November for municipal elections](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-10-07-elections/).

The EFF, Build One South Africa, ActionSA, the ANC, Rise Mzansi, uMkhonto Wesizwe (MK) party, MOVE SA, the Land Party, the African Transformation Movement (ATM) and the United Democratic Party (UDM) were in attendance.**DM**

Mark Heywood, co-founder of Union Against Hunger, opened the community engagement by highlighting that food insecurity is highest in cities in South Africa. Stunting, where a child does not receive sufficient nutrients to develop properly, affects 29% of children under five in South Africa, particularly black and poor people, he explained. As inspiration for local politicians, he cited an initiative by New York mayor Zohran Mamdani where municipal grocery stores have a 30% discount applied to core foods. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

Kabelo Khumalo, a Youth Against Hunger organiser, said South Africa is ‘in a cold war against the youth of 1976’ because they are today’s leaders. He added that South African leaders should stop using complexity regarding the issue of hunger as a reason for inaction. Youth Against Hunger is a partner organisation to Union Against Hunger. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

From left: Malik Dasoo, a food systems and environmental researcher, is the prospective councillor for wards 87 and 73, and represents Rise Mzansi; Theo Dlamini, the Johannesburg regional convenor for the MK party; and the Land Party’s mayoral candidate for Johannesburg, Nontsikelelo ‘Ntsiki’ Mazwai. ‘We have moved away from our African-ness,’ Mazwai said. She added that the country chases standards of whiteness, with pavements instead of fruit trees, and a heavy meat diet rather than a plant-based diet. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

Build One South Africa co-founder and deputy leader Nobuntu Hlazo-Webster (left), is a mayoral candidate for Johannesburg. Lubabalo Cecil Magwentshu (middle) is a senior member of the African Transformation Movement and former member of the mayoral committee for community development in Johannesburg. One thing Johannesburg should do, he said, is audit unused land and allow people to farm, along with establishing a nutritious food basket identified through wholesalers for the lowest price. Mantombi Nkosi, ANC spokesperson for the greater Gauteng region, was about to list the food security programmes the party has implemented in Johannesburg, but was drowned out by boos from the audience. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

 Nobuntu Hlazo-Webster said hunger is an outcome of a system that does not work. It is a systems problem, and an economic problem, she added. She said there is no reason that Soweto isn’t the same as Sandton. Hlazo-Webster questioned why the Soweto Fresh Produce Market is currently an empty field. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

Victor Seshoka, the national spokesperson in Gauteng for the recently formed political party MOVE SA, spoke about the importance of food gardens, land availability and use, and funding nonprofit organisations to address food security in Johannesburg. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

The UDM’s national chairperson and councillor in the City of Johannesburg, Yongama Zigebe, said the city does not need a new system, it needs the system to work. His commitment was on accountability. Zigebe said Johannesburg needs a food resilience plan to be published. Electricity, water and an affordable food basket were needed, not food parcels for the poor, or politicians posing with seeds for pictures. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

 ActionSA councillor Mpumi Edward said that opportunities for people to grow food, specifically community and backyard gardens, are currently unexplored. She also said the spaza shop sector is being ‘hijacked by illegal foreigners’. To Daily Maverick, she explained that three weeks ago they met about 300 small-scale farmers in the same community hall, to help them with seedlings and finances. She added that it is very difficult for emerging farmers to acquire unused municipal land, since there are bureaucratic hurdles and people are sent from pillar to post. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

MK party representative Theo Dlamini highlighted how important land and employment are, along with the critical role of women in ‘feeding society’. He said grants should be raised and interest-free loans given, especially to young people and women. MK would remove foreigners from the Johannesburg CBD, clean the city and solve the electricity issues in Soweto by providing solar panels to every roof. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

Rise Mzansi has a food position paper, Malik Dasoo explained. It says the Child Support Grant should be increased to meet the food poverty line, the National School Nutrition Plan should be expanded to feed children during holidays, food prices should be regulated to address market concentration, the tax on sugary beverages should be raised, and early childhood development centres should be supported. Dasoo told Daily Maverick that a ministry of food should be established – like the Department of Electricity and Energy was created – because currently the mandate is fragmented between departments and there is little interministerial cooperation. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

Thabile Mntande asked the candidates how they would support children, specifically with sufficient nutrition during early childhood, along with support for pregnant women. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

‘All of you have bellies full of food,’ said Mnino Makola from Tshwane. He asked the candidates how the country could stop selling food and move away from capitalistic modes of production and consumption. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

ATM member Ntandazo Mtebele asked the audience to take their ‘anger to the ballot box’. He said the common enemy is the ANC. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

Koketso Poho, an EFF member in the Gauteng legislature, told Daily Maverick that residents’ questions and frustrations were justified and constructive. He said municipalities should not be afraid to expropriate land for small-scale farmers, along with subsidies and incentives. ‘We have fought for more than one household per yard,’ he said regarding expanding the indigent household criteria. ‘But we are also saying for poor families, recipients of Sassa, to afford food they need to be given subsidies on water, electricity and other basic services.’ He added that their debt should be written off. He explained that the EFF-led department had provided access for small-scale farmers to supply the Johannesburg Fresh Produce Market, as well as farming cooperatives. They had also led the upgrade of clinics to provide 24-hour antenatal care and midwifery to women in Gauteng. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

Rise Mzansi member Niel Meyer spoke in his personal capacity about how the ‘middle class needs to do its bit’. He said that ‘all should feed all’ and that there should be a democratisation of food. The barriers are in our own minds, he said, referring to food security. (Photo: Lillian Roberts)

title: 特朗普宣布台湾同意购买阿拉斯加天然气，台湾：计划投资44亿美元
summary: 华盛顿 — 唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)总统星期二(10月13日)宣布，台湾已同意在未来20年内购买阿拉斯加天然气管道项目30%的天然气。台湾经济部星期三确认已经签署参与该项计划的意向书，并表示相关磋商已经取得“重大进展”。 特朗普总统在阿拉斯加的一次竞选集会上做出了上述表示，并表示，台湾将额外投资44亿美元，以确保项目完工。特朗普当时正为阿拉斯加州共和党籍现任联邦参议员丹·沙利文(Dan Sullivan)助选。在即将到来的国会中期选举，沙利文与民主党候选人玛
content:
华盛顿 —

唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)总统星期二(10月13日)宣布，台湾已同意在未来20年内购买阿拉斯加天然气管道项目30%的天然气。台湾经济部星期三确认已经签署参与该项计划的意向书，并表示相关磋商已经取得“重大进展”。

特朗普总统在阿拉斯加的一次竞选集会上做出了上述表示，并表示，台湾将额外投资44亿美元，以确保项目完工。特朗普当时正为阿拉斯加州共和党籍现任联邦参议员丹·沙利文(Dan Sullivan)助选。在即将到来的国会中期选举，沙利文与民主党候选人玛丽·佩尔托拉(Mary Peltola)的选情胶着。

“这保证了成功。这是历史上规模最大的承诺之一，也是有史以来最大的交易之一。”特朗普说。

他将这一消息的功劳归于沙利文。“我必须说，丹·沙利文帮我促成了这件事。谢谢你，丹。”特朗普说。

台湾经济部在特朗普宣布上述消息后发布一项声明。声明说，台湾中油股份有限公司去年3月与阿拉斯加天然气管线开发公司已经签署了阿拉斯加液化天然气(Alaska LNG)买卖暨投资意向书。经过一年半的“密集协商及审慎评估”，该公司已经与美国开发商取得“重大进展”。台湾中油是台湾经济部主管的国营企业。

阿拉斯加液化天然气项目预计耗资445亿到545亿美元，计划兴建一条长达800英里(1300公里)的管线，将天然气从阿拉斯加北部北坡地区(North Slope)的天然气输送至南部的安克雷奇(Anchorage)附近的液化设施，以准备出口至亚洲。当地多年来一直在力推这一项目，但是高昂的成本和对其经济可行性的质疑阻碍了项目的进展。

台湾经济部确认，该计划预计投资金额为44亿美元。一旦项目投产，台湾每年将购买600万吨天然气。项目预估最快在2032年投产。台湾表示，希望通过长期能源采购及专案投资等方式，将有助于促进天然气供应多元性，提升供应调度弹性，进一步强化台湾的能源韧性，并深化台美合作。

经济部还表示，包括股权比例和其他条款在内的具体细节仍有待确定。台北方面指出，能够通过太平洋航线将天然气直接运往台湾具有地理优势，这将有助于分散风险。

能源安全是台湾的关键问题，台湾严重依赖来自中东的石油和天然气来支撑其科技驱动型经济。

北京外交部星期三批评了液化天然气计划，称台湾的对外事务“应以一个中国原则为基础”。中国外交部发言人毛宁在被问到台湾参与阿拉斯加天然气管线项目时表示，“民进党打着‘经贸’的幌子，企图推行‘台独’，不会得逞。”

中国声称台湾是其领土的一部分，但台北的民选政府拒绝承认这一立场。

韩国是该项目中另一个重要的潜在亚洲参与者，虽然首尔和华盛顿最近在如何描述投资承诺的现状上存在分歧。

特朗普总统9月底宣布，韩国将在美国能源产业投资2000亿美元，包括投入540亿美元于筹划已久的阿拉斯加液化天然气计划。但韩国政府随后表示，尚未最后敲定。

title: 中港澳人员赴美交流暂停，参与者或面临中国当局干预胁迫
summary: 香港 — 上个月在美国总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)为中国国家主席习近平举行的欢迎仪式上，习近平宣布，将在未来5年邀请10万名美国青少年到中国交流学习。然而，由美国政府招募并资助中港澳人员访问美国的交流计划，却传出参与者遭到中国当局的干预骚扰，导致美方在今年七月暂停该项目。 美国招募并资助中方人员赴美短期交流已有数十年历史。多年来，美国每年会邀请数十名来自中国大陆和港澳人士前往美国，了解外交政策、反恐及人工智能等范畴。据了解，中国国务院前总理李克强、香港前特首
content:
香港 —

上个月在美国总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)为中国国家主席习近平举行的欢迎仪式上，习近平宣布，将在未来5年邀请10万名美国青少年到中国交流学习。然而，由美国政府招募并资助中港澳人员访问美国的交流计划，却传出参与者遭到中国当局的干预骚扰，导致美方在今年七月暂停该项目。

美国招募并资助中方人员赴美短期交流已有数十年历史。多年来，美国每年会邀请数十名来自中国大陆和港澳人士前往美国，了解外交政策、反恐及人工智能等范畴。据了解，中国国务院前总理李克强、香港前特首林郑月娥，及现任保安局局长邓炳强都曾经参与有关计划。

**香港前议员：美方根据参加者意愿安排交流**

现居美国的香港前立法会议员单仲偕于1998年首次参与由美国国务院资助的同类计划。他在接受美国之音专访时表示，美方把政治上有发展潜质的人士视为邀请对象，并根据他们的兴趣和意愿，安排整个行程。

单仲偕说：“据了解，美方希望让一些政坛新星多了解国际社会。1998年的时候，我属于政党中人，属于非政府人员。还记得当时是有关单位直接联系我的。那次我在美国至少逗留了三周，到过华盛顿、芝加哥、纽约等五、六个城市。必须强调的是，整个行程看些什么，要去哪些城市，都是参加者主导的。有关单位会根据参加者感兴趣的范畴、主题，作出行程建议。整个过程充满互动。”

虽然时隔接近三十年，单仲偕对当时为期一个月的访美交流仍然记忆犹新。

单仲偕说：“当年美国在通讯、媒体等领域一枝独秀、百花齐放。尤其留下深刻印象的是我参观了科技通讯巨头摩托罗拉，了解到美国作为科技先导者如何进行领导、监管，可谓大开眼界。这对于我往后在香港涉入相关范畴，有很大帮助。”

不过，日本《共同社》10月9日[报道](https://english.kyodonews.net/articles/-/87716)，相关的专业交流计划，包括“国际访问者领导力计划”(International Visitor Leadership Program)及“专业人才交流项目”(Professional Fellows Program)在7月底已暂停。据《共同社》掌握的一份备忘录提及，美国外交机构认为，中国当局对华府资助训练和交流的参与者施加“过度干预”，部分人在胁迫下退出，也有人遭到“骚扰、威胁，甚至被逮捕”。

美国之音就有关计划暂停向国务院发出问询请求，但至发稿前，并未收到回应。

**陈道银：中方或对参加者软硬兼施**

对于中国当局是否向有意到美国交流的人员施压，旅居智利的中国独立政治学者陈道银对美国之音表示，若真有其事，估计中方采取的手段是软硬兼施。

陈道银说：“单位只要说，‘可能不太妥当吧’，一句话就够了。参加者就知难而退了。这就是软的。如果你真的是顶得硬上的话，那就会停职，甚至现实中所有物质上的利益都没了。”

陈道银表示，中共十八大以来一再强调意识形态安全，科研院所的意识形态由一把手总负责。没有哪个一把手，就是书记，敢冒意识形态的风险。

“中国对于美国的学术交流是有加强管理的。而从美方的角度考虑，参加活动的中方人员，可能也达不到美方所需要的效果。比方说，他可能考虑到一些禁忌，一些敏感话题，就可能不再说真话了。美方也要考虑到这些人回去之后，可能受到政治压力。从这些因素考虑下来，美方暂停这个项目是不得已而为之。”陈道银说。

一名参与“专业人才交流项目”的香港人员向《共同社》透露，他在今年4月至5月到美国东岸一所大学的研究中心停留六周，其后发现自己是该计划最后一批中国参加者。

**单仲偕：国安法后，赴美交流或成“勾结外国势力”**

香港前立法会议员单仲偕估计，中国希望着眼于科技上的交流，但不愿意中方人员受到美国意识形态的影响。

单仲偕说：“中国官员当然想看(先进)科技，但这方面美方也许会有保留。但谈到意识形态、民主制度、司法独立这些，中方自然不会相信美国的一套。撇除政治和科技交流，文化领域这些中方也不热衷。在习近平治下，近年中方开始限制官员外访、外游、资产转移等。”

单仲偕说，香港主权归还中国后的最初10多年，与美国的这类交流仍然畅顺，除了民主派，亲北京政党人士也曾获邀到访美国。但自从《港版国安法》生效，过去四、五年，参与美国当局的交流活动已成为禁忌。

单仲偕说：“个别立法会议员到美国和国会议员交流，被指勾结外国势力。《国安法》生效后，在‘隐性红线’下，参与交流的人数大幅下降。而由于香港的反对派已消失，这类交流已谈不上为当地培育政坛新星。”

美国总统特朗普今年五月访问北京，并与习近平达成共识，同意建立“建设性的战略稳定关系”。上月回访美国期间，习近平在白宫的欢迎仪式上公开表示，中方未来五年将邀请10万名美国青少年到中国交流学习。

**美中互信低，人员交流难**

政治学者陈道银认为，外界不宜把中国积极邀请美国年轻人到中国观摩视为两国关系改善的指标。他说，在激烈竞争下美中将如何共存才是重点。

陈道银说：“美国是在7月份中止两个交流项目。习近平是在9月(宣布邀请美国年轻人到中国交流)。这两者当中有个时间差。美国终止了交流项目，但是中国开放对美国年轻人接触中国的渠道。美中之间的战略战争实际上还是很激烈的。从此事就可以看出，美中之间的竞争已从物理层面、科技层面，进展到知识交流层面了，也反映出两国之间的竞争在加剧。”

新加坡国立大学政治系副教授庄嘉颖对美国之音表示，美中两国仍有不少议题有待解决，包括彼此的科技限制，中国对美投资的限制等。在这种氛围下，两国元首的合作意愿能否落实，仍有待观察。

庄嘉颖说：“虽然习近平有提出，希望有更多美国年轻人去中国交流，可是在实际操作方面可能与习的话有些出入。虽然美中双方领导人之间希望表示一定的默契，不过在结构上，美中双方彼此的互信很低，互相质疑很高。(两国)领导人建立的形象是一回事，而两边实际的运作是另外一回事。”

summary: 2026 年 10 月 14 日，中国海军辽宁号航空母舰 (16) 在菲律宾海。日本联合参谋部照片 据日本联合参谋部称，截至周三，中国人民解放军海军辽宁舰航母战斗群正在菲律宾海执行任务。由 CNS 辽宁号航空母舰 (16) 率领的打击群被发现位于日本石垣岛以南 155 英里处，正在发射和回收飞机。该打击群包括辽宁舰、鞍山号巡洋舰（103艘）和无锡号巡洋舰（104艘）以及怀宁号驱逐舰（123艘）。 JSO此前于当地时间上午11点对辽宁舰进行了观测
content:
2026 年 10 月 14 日，中国海军辽宁号航空母舰 (16) 在菲律宾海。日本联合参谋部照片 据日本联合参谋部称，截至周三，中国人民解放军海军辽宁舰航母战斗群正在菲律宾海执行任务。由 CNS 辽宁号航空母舰 (16) 率领的打击群被发现位于日本石垣岛以南 155 英里处，正在发射和回收飞机。该打击群包括辽宁舰、鞍山号巡洋舰（103艘）和无锡号巡洋舰（104艘）以及怀宁号驱逐舰（123艘）。 JSO此前于当地时间周二上午11点观察到辽宁舰在东海向南航行，距离端上群岛西南约242英里。周三，该打击群在冲绳和宫古岛之间向东南航行，进入菲律宾海。日本海上自卫队驱逐舰 JS Yugiri (DD-153)、一架日本海上自卫队 P-1 海上巡逻机和一架日本海上自卫队 P-3C Orion MPA 对辽宁舰进行了监视和信息收集。为了应对航母的战斗机行动，日本航空自卫队紧急出动战斗机。辽宁舰航母战斗群包括辽宁舰、鞍山号巡洋舰（103艘）、无锡号巡洋舰（104艘）以及怀宁号驱逐舰（123艘）。该群体于 2026 年 10 月 14 日在菲律宾海被发现。日本联合参谋部照片 根据中国海军的说法，南海大队正在西太平洋地区进行例行训练，不针对任何特定国家或目标。
解放军海军新闻稿称：“10月14日，中国海军派遣辽宁舰编队赴西太平洋海域进行训练，此次训练是按照年度例行训练计划组织的，旨在检验和提高编队实战训练水平，不断增强执行任务能力。符合相关国际法和惯例，不针对任何特定国家和目标。”辽宁舰的第二次部署是在美国和日本即将开始双边“利剑27”演习的五天前进行的。“利剑27”联合综合反舰作战训练活动将在两个地点进行：四国以南和九州以东的地区以及从九州西南部延伸到冲绳岛东北部的地区。据日本《朝日新闻》报道，美国海军西奥多·罗斯福号航母战斗群预计将参加“利剑”演习。海军陆战队将在石垣岛和与那国岛部署海军-海军陆战队远征舰拦截系统（NMESIS）和TPS-80雷达。日本陆上自卫队将在石垣岛部署 12 型和 88 型移动地基地对地导弹系统，并在与那国岛部署 88 型，为“利剑”进行非实弹射击训练。日本联合参谋部于 2026 年 10 月 14 日追踪的辽宁舰航母打击群航线图。
日本联合参谋部地图 辽宁舰目前所在位置位于台湾南端以东以及台湾与菲律宾之间的吕宋海峡。 自周四以来，中国一直在从南海到东北辽宁省的五个地区沿海进行一系列军事演习。台湾地区没有举行任何演习。演习分阶段进行，预计于周六结束。台湾总统赖清德10月11日独立日讲话称中国继续

PLAN aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16) in the Philippine Sea on Oct. 14, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office photo The People’s Liberation Army Navy Liaoning Carrier Strike Group was operating in the Philippine Sea as of Wednesday, according to a Japan Joint Staff Office. Led by aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning (16), the strike group was spotted 155 miles south of Japan’s Ishigaki Island launching and recovering aircraft. The strike group includes Liaoning, cruisers CNS Anshan (103) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainen (123). The JSO previously observed the Liaoning CSG at 11 a.m. local time Tuesday sailing south in the East China Sea around 242 miles southwest of the Danjo Islands. On Wednesday, the strike group sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako Island to enter the Philippine Sea. Japan Maritime Self Defense Force destroyer JS Yugiri (DD-153), a JMSDF P-1 Maritime Patrol Aircraft and a JMSDF P-3C Orion MPA carried out surveillance and information gathering on the Liaoning CSG. In response to the carrier’s fighter operations, the Japan Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter aircraft. The Liaoning Carrier Strike Group includes Liaoning, cruisers CNS Anshan (103) and CNS Wuxi (104) and destroyer CNS Huainen (123). The group was spotted Oct. 14, 2026, in the Philippine Sea. Japan Joint Staff Office photo According to the PLAN, the CSG is conducting routine training in the Western Pacific that is not directed at any specific country or target. “On October 14, the Chinese PLA Navy sent the Liaoning Carrier task group to the waters of the Western Pacific to conduct training, which is organized in accordance with annual routine training plan, aiming to test and improve the group’s realistic training level and continuously enhance the capabilities to execute missions. It is in compliance with relevant international law and practices and not directed against any specific country or target,” reads the PLAN news release . The Liaoning CSG’s deployment, the second for the year, comes five days before the U.S. and Japan are set to begin bilateral exercise Keen Sword 27. The joint integrated anti-ship combat training event for Keen Sword will take place in two locations – in an area south of Shikoku and east of Kyushu and in an area that stretches southwest of Kyushu up to north east of Okinawa. The U.S. Navy’s Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group is expected to take part in Keen Sword, Japanese newspaper Asahi Shimbun reported . Te Marine Corps will deploy the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and TPS-80 radars to Ishigaki Island and Yonaguni Island. The Japan Ground Self-Defense Force will deploy its Type 12 and Type 88 mobile, ground-based, surface-to-surface missile systems on Ishigaki Island and the Type 88 on Yonaguni for non-live fire training for Keen Sword. Map of the Liaoning Carrier Strike Group’s route, tracked by Japan’s Joint Staff Office on Oct. 14, 2026. Japan Joint Staff Office map The Liaoning CSG’s current location is east of the southern tip of Taiwan and the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines. Since Thursday, China has been conducting a series of military drills along its coast in five areas, from the South China Sea up to the northeastern province of Liaoning. None of the drills are being held around Taiwan. The drills are being held in phases and are set to conclude on Saturday. Taiwan President Lai Ching-te in his Independence Day speech on Oct. 11 said that China continues to apply pressure through military and gray-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait. “Our aim by increasing investment in national defense is not to provoke; rather, it is to deter war. We are strengthening our self-defense not to abandon dialogue, but to ensure that dialogue can take place on the basis of parity and dignity,” Lai said. “Taiwan cherishes peace, but we will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination.” Lai’s speech was denounced by China Ministry of National Defense spokesperson Snr. Col. Chen Xi. “The PLA’s routine military exercises around Taiwan are a natural and justifiable way to deter any reckless actions by ‘Taiwan independence’ advocates and attempts at foreign interference, and to safeguard the safety and well-being of the Taiwanese people,” said Chen, according to a transcript . China has not announced any drills around Taiwan in response to Lai’s speech. The PLAN has not said how long the Liaoning CSG will be deployed or where it will operate. The Liaoning CSG previously carried out a 40-day deployment from May to June, returning to its homeport of Qingdao on June 22.

Hong Kong's Marine Department said on Wednesday that applications for the 'Guangdong Yacht Southbound' scheme are now open, ahead of the first voyage on Friday. Under the scheme, owners or captains of Guangdong-registered yachts wishing to sail south to Hong Kong can complete cross-border procedures as early as 30 days before arrival.

Applicants must submit online declarations to Hong Kong authorities at least 30 hours before arriving in the city, and to mainland authorities at least four hours before departing mainland waters, the department said.

The scheme is part of broader efforts by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government to facilitate yacht travel between Guangdong and Hong Kong. Over the past few months, authorities have trained and assessed mainland captains on their knowledge of Hong Kong waters, according to earlier government statements.

The Marine Department has also set up a real-time yacht movement monitoring system to assist with berthing arrangements for Guangdong yachts. In addition, an electronic business system has been introduced to provide one-stop convenience services for crew members and passengers travelling on these vessels.

The first voyage under the scheme is scheduled for Friday, marking the start of regular operations.

title: The strongman finally meets a stronger institution
summary: _**First of a four-part series**_ TODAY the Deegong sits in detention at The Hague, confronting an institution he neither appoints, finances nor frightens. The ICC has confirmed the charges arising from killings allegedly committed during h
content:
_**First of a four-part series**_

TODAY the Deegong sits in detention at The Hague, confronting an institution he neither appoints, finances nor frightens. The ICC has confirmed the charges arising from killings allegedly committed during his drug wars. It has now ruled him mentally and physically fit to stand trial starting Nov. 30.

For the first time, Duterte faces a court where profanity is not policy, popularity is not evidence and threats settle nothing. At 81, time is scarce. Tatay Deegong may never come home!

*   [From parking lots to people places](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/14/opinion/columns/from-parking-lots-to-people-places/2444795)

**The man and the myth**

Duterte understood the Filipino mood. People were weary of crime, corruption, drugs, and leaders who spoke magnificently while achieving remarkably little. He promised decisive action. Where others commissioned studies, he promised bodies. Government looked helpless, justice moved slowly and criminals seemed shielded by lawyers and connections. His impatient remedy was simple: Eliminate the problem, debate legality later. He was a leader who burst into the scene possessing no moral scruples.

He styled himself as a probinsyano outsider, unsullied by Manila manners. His curses, threats and killing jokes separated him from polished politicians who had disappointed the country. Even his misogyny somehow sailed past many feminists.

The performance worked, especially among his Davao constituents. Biliba gyud oi!

Filipinos elected more than a president. They chose an avenging Tatay and granted him extraordinary freedom to punish anyone he declared an enemy. The trouble with national fathers is that citizens become obedient children, mistaking submission for loyalty.

*   ![Image 1: Laguna mayors rally behind Aragones](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/14/1257533.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Laguna mayors rally behind Aragones](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/14/regions/laguna-mayors-rally-behind-aragones/2444954)

**The imperial president**

Years ago, during an interview he granted me in Malacañang, I described Duterte as an imperial president — not because the Constitution crowned him emperor, but because our institutions behaved as though it had.

Duterte did not invent the imperial presidency. Our unitary-presidential system built it — concentrating power in one man while expecting dependent institutions to restrain him. Thus, our celebrated checks and balances: everyone checks where power lies. Duterte simply mastered the machinery. (I gave him copies of my Harvard professor Graham Allison’s Destined for War and Schlessinger’s The Imperial Presidency.)

Congress surrendered its independence. Parties became employment agencies, Cabinet officials paid obeisance. Presidential threats encouraged violent shortcuts. Human rights were mocked and critics intimidated.

*   ![Image 2: Marcos’ impeachment plot backfires](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/13/1258203.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Marcos’ impeachment plot backfires](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/14/opinion/columns/marcos-impeachment-plot-backfires/2444878)

**The war that refused to end**

He promised to eliminate drugs within months. Subsequently, he admitted the problem exceeded his campaign bravado. By then, thousands were dead.

Official and human-rights estimates differed enormously. But behind every number was a person killed and a family asking whether the victim had been investigated and convicted — or merely identified, pursued and silenced.

Duterte’s defenders insist the campaign protected citizens from criminals and that police confronted armed suspects in self-defense. They accuse the ICC of violating Philippine sovereignty. Those arguments must be heard. Due process belongs equally to victims and Duterte.

*   ![Image 3: Pangilinan seeks reversal of ruling on Duterte’s dropped charges](https://miopia.newsroom.bi/statics/i/ps/manilatimes.net/manilatimes/uploads/images/2026/10/14/1258438.jpg?width=113&crop=113:85)
[Pangilinan seeks reversal of ruling on Duterte’s dropped charges](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/14/news/pangilinan-seeks-reversal-of-ruling-on-dutertes-dropped-charges/2445025)

Duterte must be presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt. The ICC must prove not only that killings occurred, but that he was personally responsible. This high standard protects justice from becoming another drug war — label the accused evil, then ignore due process.

**Another trial, another shadow**

While Tatay Deegong prepares at The Hague, daughter Sara’s impeachment trial has pulled him into another controversy. Evidence presented to the Senate impeachment court identified joint accounts belonging to Sara and Rodrigo Duterte. Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records described roughly P193 million in transactions in one day; one particular joint account recorded two transactions totaling P18.9 million.

These figures are being tested in Sara’s trial. They do not prove that either Duterte stole or laundered money. A joint account is not a conviction. Money can travel through a bank without acquiring handcuffs.

But the evidence raises questions that indignation cannot answer. Where did the money come from? Why was it moved? Was it declared? Did it correspond with legitimate income and assets?

Sara must be allowed to challenge the records; Rodrigo deserves the same presumption of innocence. But the man who demanded dismissals upon a mere “whiff of corruption” can hardly complain when the public smells a stronger aroma.

The cases are legally separate. Politically, however, they raise the same question: how Duterte gained power, used it and avoided scrutiny while in office.

We will return to the financial evidence later in our series. For now, the Hague is no longer the only courtroom casting a shadow over the Deegong.

The newer evidence matters because Duterte presented himself as the incorruptible scourge of thieves. He publicly humiliated officials, dismissed some upon suspicion and repeatedly promised that even a “whiff of corruption” was enough. Yet Pharmally, the POGOs, Michael Yang and other controversies already weakened that immaculate image. The joint accounts now raise a more personal question. Did the president who claimed to smell corruption everywhere somehow lose his celebrated sense of smell when the financial trail approached his own family? Again, questions are not proof — but neither are they persecution.

**Justice or political revenge**

Duterte’s supporters see persecution and revenge by enemies unable to defeat his popularity. They are not entirely irrational. The Marcos-Duterte alliance collapsed into dynastic warfare. Former friends became prosecutors. The government that once resisted ICC cooperation delivered Duterte to The Hague.

Politics is present. It is practically dancing on the courtroom steps. But political motive does not automatically erase legal responsibility. A thief exposed by another thief does not become innocent because his accuser also requires investigation.

Marcos obviously benefited from the Deegong’s removal. The question is whether admissible evidence proves the charges. Every president must face the same standard. Otherwise, accountability becomes the weapon of whichever dynasty controls Malacañang.

**The limits of popularity**

Tatay remains loved by millions. Supporters remember infrastructure, decisive leadership and contempt for Manila elites. To many Mindanaoans, his prosecution feels like another distant judgment against a leader who gave the South national importance. That sentiment cannot simply be mocked.

But popularity is not acquittal. Elections choose who governs; they legalize nothing afterward. If 60 percent approve a killing, the victim does not become 40 percent less dead. Democracy without the rule of law is merely majority appetite armed with the power of the State.

**The real defendant**

Duterte is accused, but our political system is also on trial. It produced a president powerful enough to terrify domestic institutions, leaving accountability to a foreign court. His daughter’s impeachment is revealing financial questions during his presidency. We should neither defend Duterte completely nor condemn him before the evidence is heard.

Let prosecutors prove their case, Duterte contest it, and judges decide without orders from Manila, Washington, Beijing, or Davao.

The verdict will determine Duterte’s legal responsibility. It will not repair the institutions that failed before The Hague intervened. That work remains ours.

The strongman has finally met an institution he cannot command. The question is whether the Philippines will learn to build institutions just as strong before we elect another one.

Next week, we return to our geopolitical series, “When the referee retreats — the vacuum never remains empty,” examining the repercussions for smaller nations like ours. Then, back to the Dutertes: the father confronting international justice; the daughter facing impeachment and preparing for the presidency.

_To be continued_

_lito.lorenzana@cdpi.asia_

title: Nigeria: U.S. Lists Nigeria Among 14 Countries Facing Military Aid Cuts
summary: The United States has listed Nigeria among 14 countries facing potential cuts to military assistance over the recruitment and use of child soldiers, a designation that could affect defence cooperation, military training and weapons sales. T
content:
The United States has listed Nigeria among 14 countries facing potential cuts to military assistance over the recruitment and use of child soldiers, a designation that could affect defence cooperation, military training and weapons sales.

The designation was contained in the US State Department's 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report, published on October 11, which identified Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) as armed groups continuing to recruit, abduct and use children in Nigeria.

The report covers the period from April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026, and places Nigeria on the Child Soldiers Prevention Act (CSPA) list alongside Afghanistan, Burma, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Iran, Russia, Rwanda, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Venezuela and Yemen.

Follow us on [WhatsApp](https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VaIdDi8Bqbr263erhw1K "https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VaIdDi8Bqbr263erhw1K") | [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/allafrica/ "https://www.linkedin.com/company/allafrica/") for the latest headlines

Under the CSPA, countries on the list may face restrictions on certain forms of US security assistance and the commercial licensing of military equipment, subject to applicable exceptions, a presidential waiver or other provisions under the law.

The report stated that the restrictions would take effect from October 1, 2026, and apply throughout the relevant fiscal year unless an exemption or waiver was granted.

"The CSPA prohibits assistance to governments that are identified in the list under the following authorities: International Military Education and Training, Foreign Military Financing, Excess Defence Articles, and Peacekeeping Operations, with exceptions for some programs undertaken pursuant to the Peacekeeping Operations authority.

"The CSPA also prohibits the issuance of licenses for direct commercial sales of military equipment to such governments," the report stated.

The designation comes amid continued security cooperation between Washington and Abuja, including joint efforts to combat terrorism and other security threats in Nigeria.

According to the report, Boko Haram and ISWAP continue to recruit, abduct and use children as young as 12 in various roles, including as cooks, domestic workers, spies, porters, messengers, bodyguards, checkpoint guards, armed combatants and suicide bombers.

The groups reportedly operate across Nigeria, Cameroon, Chad and Niger, subjecting children to physical and sexual abuse and forced drug use.

"Boko Haram and ISIS-West Africa continue recruiting, abducting, and using--including through force, fraud, and coercion--child soldiers as young as 12 years old as cooks, domestic workers, spies, porters, messengers, bodyguards or guards at checkpoints, 'morality police,' armed combatants, and suicide bombers in attacks in Nigeria, Cameroon, Chad, and Niger; these children are subjected to physical and sexual abuse and forced drug use," the report stated.

Get the latest in African news delivered straight to your inbox

The report also raised concerns over the abduction and exploitation of women and girls in northern Nigeria, including forced labour, domestic servitude, sexual slavery and forced marriage.

It alleged that Boko Haram had kidnapped thousands of women and girls and forced some into marriages, while punishing girls who refused to marry by compelling them to become suicide bombers.

Beyond insurgent groups, the report said criminal gangs in southern Nigeria recruit children for forced criminal activities, including kidnappings and robberies, while exploiting some in sex trafficking.

It also identified forced labour in agriculture and mining as a concern involving criminal gangs in the north-west.

Apart from the child-soldier designation, the report said Nigeria had failed to meet the minimum standards for eliminating trafficking for the 15th consecutive year, although it acknowledged some improvements in government funding and victim support.

The US State Department expressed concern over alleged official complicity in trafficking crimes, stating that the Nigerian government did not report investigations, prosecutions or convictions of public officials allegedly involved in such offences during the reporting period.

"The government did not report any investigations, prosecutions, or convictions of government employees allegedly complicit in trafficking crimes or provide details or other actions taken against complicit officials from previous years," the report stated.

It added that "corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes remained significant concerns."

Nigerian soldiers

13 October 2026

[Premium Times (Abuja)](http://premiumtimesng.com/ "Visit Premium Times (Abuja)")

By Yakubu Mohammed

_The listing places pressure on the Nigerian government to address concerns over child recruitment and demonstrate compliance with international standards on the protection of children in armed conflict._

The United States has placed Nigeria on its 2026 list of countries whose governments are identified as having armed forces, security forces or government-supported militias that recruit or use child soldiers, exposing the country to restrictions on certain US military assistance and equipment sales.

The designation, contained in the US State Department's 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report, means Nigeria could face restrictions on specific security assistance and commercial licences for military equipment from 1 October, unless the restrictions are waived or an applicable exception is granted by US President Donald Trump.

Nigeria is among 14 countries included on the 2026 Child Soldiers Prevention Act (CSPA) list, alongside Afghanistan, Burma, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Iran, Russia, Rwanda, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Venezuela and Yemen.

Under Section 402 of the CSPA, the US government identifies foreign governments whose armed forces, police, other security forces or government-supported armed groups allegedly recruit or use child soldiers. The latest determinations cover 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026.

The law prohibits certain forms of assistance to listed governments, including International Military Education and Training, Foreign Military Financing and Excess Defence Articles. It also restricts the issuance of licences for direct commercial sales of military equipment, subject to applicable exceptions and presidential waivers.

The restrictions could have implications for Nigeria's military cooperation with Washington, particularly in areas involving training, financing and the acquisition of US military equipment.

The State Department said its determination draws on multiple sources, including observations by US government personnel, United Nations agencies, international organisations, civil society groups and local and international media reports.

Under the CSPA, a child soldier includes anyone under 18 who is compulsorily recruited into government armed forces or security forces, as well as children recruited or used in hostilities by armed forces distinct from a state's military.

The definition also covers children serving in support roles, including as cooks, porters, messengers, medics, guards or victims of sexual exploitation.

Nigeria's inclusion on the list comes amid longstanding concerns about the recruitment and exploitation of children in the country's conflict zones, particularly in the North-east, where Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) have abducted and recruited children for combat and support roles.
